analysis.one_liner: Creates a national database of health care claims and prices that patients, employers, and researchers could access.
analysis.headline: The bill died two weeks after it was introduced: with no cosponsors, it was referred to five House committees and never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the government to hire a nonprofit to build a national database of health care claims and payments, collecting data from every private insurer plus Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and the federal employee health plan. Patients, employers, researchers, and states could access the data cheaply or for free, and the database would publish yearly reports on price trends and regional cost differences. The goal is to let everyone see what care actually costs, which researchers and policymakers could use to push prices down.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, employers who sponsor health plans, independent researchers, and state governments gain access to detailed data on what health care actually costs across the country. The bill requires the database to publish reports on price trends, access gaps, and regional cost differences for free, and to make underlying data available to patients, providers, employers, and researchers at no more than cost. Congress and federal agencies also get a tool for evaluating health care spending that does not currently exist at the national level.

how_it_helps.text: Gives patients, employers, providers, and independent researchers access to national health care claims and payment data at cost or for free, data that is currently held privately by insurers and largely unavailable.
Requires annual public reports on health care price trends, coverage and service costs, access gaps, and geographic differences, so the public and Congress can see where prices are highest.

Requires Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and the federal employee health plan to submit their claims data too, giving a complete picture of American health care spending across both public and private coverage.
Offers federal grants of up to $10 million per state to build or expand state-level all-payer claims databases that feed into the national one.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, employer group health plans, pharmacy benefit managers, and third-party administrators would bear the cost of electronically submitting all their claims data, including prescription drug and substance-use-treatment claims, in a standardized format. Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and the federal employee health program would also have to turn over their claims data. The public pays for the database itself: the bill appropriates $50 million per year to run it, plus up to $40 million per year in grants to states.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: The bill shields 'proprietary financial information' and exempts the submitted data from public disclosure laws and from use as evidence in court or administrative proceedings, so the negotiated contract rates behind many prices would remain partially hidden even under a transparency database.

Insurers, employers, and administrators would face real compliance costs to reformat and submit all their claims data, and the bill authorizes $90 million per year in combined federal spending, which supporters would need to justify.

The bill relies on a single contracted nonprofit entity to build and run the database, with an initial 10-year contract term, creating a potential single point of failure for a system holding sensitive health data on nearly all Americans.
A national database shows where prices differ but does not itself lower them; turning transparency into lower costs would require separate action by regulators, employers, or Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: a functioning national all-payer claims database would give employers, patients, researchers, and policymakers visibility into health care prices that no public body has today, and comparable state databases have already been used to identify cost drivers. The design has genuine weaknesses, especially the carve-outs that exempt negotiated contract terms from disclosure and bar the data from use in legal proceedings, which would blunt some of the transparency the bill promises. But those weaknesses were never tested, because the bill never got any consideration at all: it was introduced in the last days of a Congress with no cosponsors and no committee action, so the trade-off voters actually got was no database versus a flawed-but-real one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the final days of the 117th Congress, referred to five committees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended two weeks later.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Beyer introduced the National All-Payer Claims Database Act of 2022 on December 21, 2022, with no cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to five committees the same day: Energy and Commerce, plus Ways and Means, Oversight and Reform, Education and Labor, and Armed Services.
No committee held a hearing or markup, the House never voted on the bill, and the Senate never considered it. The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and other payers are better off because the bill never advanced: they avoid a federal mandate to hand over their full claims data. Patients, employers, and researchers gained nothing, and remain without a national claims database.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted support beyond its single Democratic sponsor, so the outcome reflects an absence of cross-party or cross-member buy-in rather than a recorded partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers and plans to submit all claims data, including prescription drug claims, to a national database that patients, employers, and researchers could use to see what they are charging. It bars them from placing any restrictions on how that data is used.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and third-party administrators
industries.note: Pharmacy benefit managers and third-party administrators act as the submission channel for group health plans, so the bill's mandatory reporting and its prohibition on restricting data use apply directly to them.

Claims data would reveal payment patterns across providers, exposing price variation. The bill tries to soften this by defining 'proprietary financial information' to exclude the actual billing and payment amounts in claims, but negotiated contract terms would still be shielded from other providers.

The bill appropriates $50 million per year to operate the database and authorizes $40 million per year in state grants, creating a large, long-term federal funding stream for a single contracted nonprofit entity with an initial 10-year contract term.
